chunks: Design a memory cell. The question: Design a memory cell.
First ask what you need: speed, density and standby power. For fast memory inside a processor chip, the answer is the SRAM cell.
A loop of two inverters holds the bit, and two access transistors connect it to the bit lines for reading and writing.
For dense main memory, the answer is a DRAM cell, one transistor and one capacitor.
A rocker switch stays where you leave it, as long as it has power, which is SRAM.
A bucket with a tiny leak holds water for a while, but you must top it up regularly, which is DRAM. The bucket is smaller, so you fit billions.
The bucket picture misses that reading a DRAM cell drains it, so the value must be written back.
Net labels with the same name are connected.
Node Q (between MP1 and MN1) is wired straight to the gates of MP2/MN2, and node Q̄ (between MP2 and MN2) returns to the gates of MP1/MN1 through the matching Q̄ labels: that is the bistable loop.
MA1 and MA2 connect Q and Q̄ to BL and BLB, and share the word line WL.
SRAM: static RAM. Each bit sits in a loop of two inverters (gates whose output is the opposite of their input), each feeding the other. It needs no refresh. DRAM: dynamic RAM.
Each bit is charge on a tiny capacitor, which leaks. Word line and bit line: the word line selects a row of cells. Bit lines carry the data to and from them.
Access transistor: a switch that connects a storage node to a bit line when the word line is on.
Refresh: periodically reading and rewriting DRAM cells before their charge leaks away.
An SRAM cell has 4 transistors in the inverter loop plus 2 access transistors, 6 in all. To write, drive the bit lines and turn on the word line; they overpower the loop.
Now a DRAM read. Say the supply is 1. 2 volts, the cell capacitor is 25 fF (femtofarads, a tiny capacitance), and the bit line is 100 fF, precharged to 0. 6 volts.
A stored 1 shares charge and moves the bit line by 0. 12 volts, or 120 millivolts, which a sensitive amplifier (the sense amplifier) detects.
"I'd first ask volatile or not, and speed versus density.
For fast on-chip storage I'd use a 6T SRAM cell: two cross-coupled CMOS inverters hold the bit, and two NMOS access transistors on a word line connect the storage nodes to the bit lines.
Write by driving the bit lines and overpowering the cell; read by precharging and sensing which line droops.
Sizing is the trade-off: the pull-downs must beat the access devices for read stability, and the access devices must beat the pull-ups for write.
For density I'd use a 1T1C DRAM cell, which needs refresh."
